title: The Pearl in the Sea: How the Soul-Body is Molded into a New Man by Drops from Above
arc: The teaching opens with the cosmic-man whose members correspond to the cosmos and then unfolds the pearl analogy — heavenly drops falling into receptive oysters in particular places of the sea — to teach how the soul wearing a body is molded into a New Man when the Mind of Light, Wisdom, and Hearing descend upon it through the food and water it receives, and how the same body becomes a place of disturbance when the bitter members and lower wells flow in instead.
reading:
This teaching is a single sustained correspondence between a cosmological body, a pearl forming in the sea, and the human soul-in-body being shaped into the New Man. The opening section, though heavily damaged, sets the frame: there is an Old Man on one side and on the other a figure "perfected in his members," a Youth and small king of beautiful likeness, the Protomē "sent forth," manifesting and revealing herself. This is the standard Manichaean disclosure of the cosmic-man whose members are the receptacles of redemption — the Divine Human in his sent-forth aspect, opposite the proprium. Everything that follows is read against this body.

The teacher then asks the central question: how do pearls come to be? The answer is precise and is the spine of the whole teaching. Pearls are not molded everywhere in the sea but only in certain places, where a particular conjunction occurs. From above, sweet rain-drops fall — not as one solid stream but divided, scattered into many drops, each carrying its sweetness down through the air. They descend into the sea, sink down to the oyster, and mingle with sweet waters already there. The oyster receives them and within itself molds the pearl. Sometimes a single drop, received whole, produces one great honored Iaos-gem whose splendor is complete. Sometimes two drops join before either is fragmented, and the oyster fashions a pair within. Sometimes a single drop divides into very small fragments and many lesser pearls multiply in the shell. The oyster itself comes to be through the kek and kobe and the sea, so that every level of the formation is itself molded by what lies above it. Finally, divers — each according to his appointed lot — go down into the abyss of the sea and bring up myriads of pearls for kings and magnates.

This natural picture is the entire cosmology of regeneration in miniature. The sea is the natural mind in its receptive depth, salty and mingled. The oyster is the body — particularly the body as eating-and-drinking receptacle, "wearing" the soul. The sweet rain falling from above is the influx of Divine Truth from the heavenly members; the sweet waters already in the sea are the natural truths the soul has received and held. The pearl is the soul itself as refined truth, the gem produced where heavenly drop and natural shell meet. That pearls form only in particular places and only when the drop is received intact teaches that regeneration is local and occasional, dependent on the right conjunction of influx and receptivity. That a single whole drop produces the great Iaos-gem while a fragmented drop produces many small pearls quietly grades the kinds of regenerate state: the integral reception of Divine Truth produces one fully glorious soul; partial reception still produces real pearls, but lesser. The divers who lift them out for kings and magnates are the operations of the Lord that raise the refined soul out of the natural depth into the heavenly states.

The teaching then turns explicitly to the soul "which wears the body." When the Mind of Light comes upon her in the power of Wisdom together with the Hearing — that is, when the illumined rational understanding, Divine Wisdom, and the soul's receptive response to the Call all arrive together — he establishes her, purifies her, and makes her into a New Man, with no disturbance, no shock, no upheaval. This is the pearl-state: the heavenly drop has entered the oyster intact and the gem is forming in stillness.

But the teaching is honest about the opposite condition. When a tarachē — a disturbance — arises, the stars on high revolve around the man and shake him, stirring desire, bitterness, grief, and lupē. Whether he wills it or not, the powers of the natural heavens disturb the good things firmly set in his heart. There are also times when those upper powers are still and at rest from him, but then the disturbance enters another way: through the food he ate and the water he drank. The bitter members descend into the body together with food, mingling with the bitter members of the body and with the Sin that dwells in him, passing into bitterness, desire, grief, lupē, and the wicked reflections of the body. And there are times when the food itself comes in established and select, when the air above is still, the icon at rest, and the food bears the man upward — when the living member that abounds with the light of the souls multiplies in him, the honored ones within him have completed their changes, their soul has soared inward and become yokefellow with the living souls within him, and they bear him up while he stays sound in body, his works appointed, his teachings established, his words ordered, his soul mounted up like a bird.

So the whole second half of the teaching is a careful diagnostic. The same body is either an oyster molding a pearl or a sea churned by bitter influx. The decisive question is which "wells" are flowing into it: the wells of the upper place — the channels of influx from the heavenly members carrying light and life — or the wells of the lower place, the bitter members rising into the soul through bad eating, deceitful teachings, slack thoughts, and wicked counsels. When the upper wells flow, the soul is still, the food is select, the heart rests in its place, and the pearl is being molded. When the lower wells flow, the mind is in the place of disturbance, bitterness mingles with desire and grief, and what should have become a gem becomes only the agitated salt of the sea.

The unity of the teaching is therefore this: every human body is, in its very structure, a pearl-forming shell at the bottom of the cosmic sea. The drops that fall into it are Divine Truth in its descent — through Mind of Light, Wisdom, the Hearing, and the food and water that carry the upper members downward. The shell either receives the drop whole and in stillness, in which case the New Man is molded as a single honored gem; or it receives only fragments, in which case lesser pearls still form; or it is overrun by the bitter wells from below, in which case the soul is shaken by the very members it should have been refining. The Lord's diver eventually raises every true pearl up out of the abyss to the kings of the upper place. The teaching's practical force is that the disciple should recognize, in the moment of eating, drinking, hearing, and thinking, which wells are flowing — and so know whether at this hour his body is an oyster making a pearl or a sea making salt.
